## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

At the end of the narrative, following the revelation of the Four Noble Truths, the monk attains arahantship, and the Buddha identifies himself as the peacock king (*morarājā*) [Fausböll 1887].

Scholarly discussion also observes that the prose commentary mentions snakes among the perils from which the peacock remains free, comparing the figure of the peacock-king to related narratives such as the Suvarṇāvabhāsa account in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya [Schmithausen, Maitri magic]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus reflects 21 matching passages (3,883 characters) shared with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Catuttho bhāgo), while no cross-language matches are registered in the automated corpus [DharmaNexus].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Catuttho bhāgo) (Atk S0513a4) (§1.4–4.4 ↔ §3206–3217)
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus parallel match database for Ja 491 — Provided text-reuse data with the Pali Jātaka commentary and absence of cross-language matches.
- [Fausböll 1887] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 4 (1887) — Confirmed opening and concluding formulas, including the backsliding monk's realization of arahantship and the Bodhisatta identification.
- [Schmithausen, Maitri magic] Lambert Schmithausen, Maitrī and Magic: Aspects of the Buddhist Attitude Towards Dangerous Animals — Noted the commentary's mention of snake dangers and compared the text with peacock-king stories in Sanskrit Vinaya literature.
